The reviewer describes a merge game whose board has become gridlocked because too many items must fit on a small board. The later archiving feature does not solve the capacity problem because archived items still consume inventory space, leaving the player with insufficient storage for continued play. This is a realized inventory-capacity shortfall and supports Waste Aversion. The mention of insufficient energy describes a limited resource but does not state a recharge timer or waiting schedule, so it does not support Playing by Appointment. The complaint that the game differs from its ad concerns out-of-game advertising and is excluded under R13. The references to merging, unlocking items, and gems do not by themselves establish grinding, collection compulsion, or real-money currency conversion.

labels.label: M_WasteAversion
labels.span: game is now gridlocked. Way too many new things on a tiny board. Ridiculous. Update: they finally started "archiving" but expect you to use your inventory space for them???
labels.rationale: The board is blocked by too many items, and the supposed archiving solution still consumes limited inventory space, creating a concrete storage shortfall.

parsed.analysis: The review describes an in-game advertisement mechanic: an ad is forced after every over, requiring the player to encounter it during normal cricket gameplay. The app closing when the ad is accidentally tapped is attributed to bad app behavior and is a technical malfunction, so it does not establish a separate dark-pattern label. The request to fix the UI is hypothetical and does not describe a confirmed UI-misdirection mechanism such as a hidden or undersized cancel control.

labels.label: T_Advertisement
labels.span: After every over, an ad pops up.
labels.rationale: Ads are automatically shown at a fixed in-game event, compelling the player to view them during play.

The player is required to interact with the advertisement and enter the app store to exit it, so the ad is not merely mentioned but functions as a forced interruption. Although the reviewer says this happened incorrectly, the underlying rule is still a daily reward or streak system that penalizes missing a day, so the bug attribution does not suppress the label.

labels.rule_applied: definition; R11 exception for a malfunction triggering an underlying streak-reset penalty
labels.rationale: A streak that resets progress when the game records a missed day is a daily-return incentive with an active penalty, even though the reviewer says the reset was erroneous.

The password and username recovery process also fails by saying the information cannot be found. These are bugs or account-access errors, not deliberate game design behaviors. The review reports several complaints but only one clearly describes a coded mechanic. The statement about cheating describes other players' conduct and does not say the game rewards or incentivizes cheating. Peg-E and the race car game are named events, but no specific event mechanic is described. Gold duplicates indicate unwanted sticker copies, but the review does not describe the randomized delivery process or a compulsion to complete the collection. The complaint about limited daily trades does describe an in-game exchange of stickers with other players; a search confirms that MONOPOLY GO! treats duplicate stickers as tradable with friends and imposes a daily trade limit. That supports Reciprocity. The lack of dice is resource scarcity alone and does not establish a listed label.

labels.label: S_Reciprocity
labels.span: Not enough trades a day!
labels.rationale: The span describes a capped mechanic for trading resources with other players, which is an exchange-based favor mechanism.

parsed.search_result: The search established that duplicate stickers in MONOPOLY GO! can be traded with friends and that the game imposes a daily trade limit, supporting the interpretation of 'trades' as player-to-player resource exchange. ([monopolygo.helpshift.com](https://monopolygo.helpshift.com/hc/en/3-monopoly-go/faq/276-duplicate-stickers/?pubDate=20250530&utm_source=openai))

parsed.analysis: The review describes a competitive Ludo game in which the player plays against opponents. It also alleges that outcomes are deliberately manipulated: the player is supposedly meant to lose regardless of skill, with opponents receiving favorable dice counts while the reviewer receives unfavorable small counts. This is a claim that the game determines or tunes outcomes unfairly, which fits Illusion of Control. The separate mention of glitches is a technical complaint and does not itself create a dark-pattern label.

labels.label: S_Competition
labels.span: the opponents get good counts and you get small counts
labels.rationale: The span explicitly describes the player competing against opponents in the game.

labels.label: P_IllusionOfControl
labels.span: if you are meant to lose, no matter how good you play you will definitley lose and in most of the cases this is the scene always..the opponents get good counts and you get small counts
labels.rationale: The reviewer alleges that the game fixes or manipulates dice outcomes so the player loses regardless of skill and opponents receive better counts.

parsed.analysis: The review describes Gardenscapes as an in-game match-three puzzle structure rather than the escape gameplay shown in advertising. The misleading advertisement is outside the app-design scope under R13, so it does not receive a label. Within the game, Austin's progress is tied to repeatedly playing the puzzle game to earn stars, and each game yields only one star; this names a repetitive activity required for character progress, supporting Grinding. The loss of points after failing a level is a failure penalty, but it does not describe a retention mechanic based on accumulated investment or a real-world time gate.

labels.label: T_Grinding
labels.span: Even for walking Austin you will have to earn a star by playing stupid game.
labels.rule_applied: vs Slow Progress; the span identifies the repeated game activity and ties it to progress
labels.rationale: The player must repeatedly play the puzzle game to earn stars and advance Austin, which is a tedious task cycle required for progress.

Gathering resources is not described as repetitive or tied to a specific required progress cycle, and scouting other bases does not by itself establish competition.

The review describes a level-entry resource system. Each level consumes credits, and the increasing cost leaves the player unable to continue for an hour unless they pay cash for more credits. The hour-long wait is an in-game timer that schedules when play can resume, supporting Playing by Appointment. Paying cash to obtain credits bypasses that access barrier, supporting Pay to Progress and Intermediate Currency because real money is converted into in-game credits. The example of needing 2.8k per level describes escalating cost, but does not by itself establish another coded mechanic.

labels.label: T_PlayingByAppointment
labels.span: levels cost too much to play, which leaves you waiting an hour to play again
labels.rationale: The game imposes a one-hour timer before the player can resume playing.

labels.rule_applied: Pay to Skip; spend money to avoid waiting for a timer to expire
labels.rationale: The player can pay for credits to bypass the barrier that otherwise prevents continued level play.

labels.rationale: The span describes exchanging real-world cash for in-game credits used to play levels.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer describes a 7-day streak that is lost when the game registers a problem, and they report this has happened three times. A streak is a daily-return reward mechanic with a penalty for losing accumulated progress, so this supports Daily Rewards. Although the reviewer says it happened for no reason and treats it as an issue, R11 allows the label because the underlying streak-reset rule is still the relevant game design behavior.

labels.label: T_DailyRewards
labels.span: I've had 3 separate times times to where I've lost my 7 day streak for no reason whatsoever
labels.rule_applied: definition; R11 bug attribution does not suppress the underlying streak-reset penalty
labels.rationale: A 7-day streak that can be lost is a daily-return incentive with an explicit penalty for losing accumulated progress.

parsed.analysis: The review describes a daily mission system that limits what can be completed within the available attempts, implying a recurring daily task structure. It also describes an in-game timer that takes nearly two minutes to restore new chances to play, which imposes a wait before gameplay can continue. The complaint that items do not appear according to orders describes an unfavorable or possibly malfunctioning outcome, but it does not clearly establish a coded dark-pattern mechanic.

labels.label: T_DailyRewards
labels.span: The daily missions are impossible to do in such less attempts
labels.rule_applied: Daily task lists with resetting rewards
labels.rationale: The span identifies a daily mission system that constrains the player's tasks within a recurring daily cycle.

labels.label: T_PlayingByAppointment
labels.span: it takes nearly 2 minutes for new chances to play
labels.rationale: New chances are restored only after an in-game timer, forcing the player to wait before playing again.

parsed.analysis: The review describes a casino slot game that is intentionally engaging but offers extremely poor chances of winning. The reviewer explicitly refers to returning to spend more money, so real money is being used in a luck-based game, which supports Gambling. However, the statement that winning is impossible is only a general complaint about outcomes; it does not describe rigging, near-misses, a fixed schedule, or a specific reward-delivery mechanism. It therefore does not support Illusion of Control, Optimism and Frequency Biases, or Reward Mania.

labels.label: M_Gambling
labels.span: why would I ever come back and spend more money when it is impossible to when
labels.rationale: The reviewer describes spending more money in a casino slots app, linking real-money participation to a luck-based chance game.
